Physiology.question: ১) What is not the example of transcellular fluid-?
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Oedema fluid. It is an interstitial fluid, formed by excessive accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space, and is not a transcellular fluid.

Transcellular fluid is a specialized component of the extracellular fluid (ECF) enclosed by epithelial membranes. Examples include:

  • CSF

  • Aqueous humor

  • Synovial fluid

  • Pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal fluids

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) CSF – A classic transcellular fluid.

  • গ) Aqueous humor – A transcellular fluid.

  • ঘ) Urine – Although urine is not generally classified as part of the body's ECF after excretion, exam questions asking about body fluid compartments typically distinguish oedema fluid as interstitial rather than transcellular.

High-yield points:

  • ECF = Plasma + Interstitial fluid + Transcellular fluid

  • Transcellular fluids: CSF, aqueous humor, synovial, pleural, pericardial, peritoneal fluids

  • Oedema fluid = Interstitial fluid (not transcellular)

Physiology.question: ২) Compared with intracellular fluid, extra-cellular fluid has
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is ঘ) a lower potassium ion concentration.

Compared with intracellular fluid (ICF), extracellular fluid (ECF) contains:

  • Much lower K⁺ concentration

  • Much higher Na⁺ and Cl⁻ concentrations

  • Similar osmolarity (~285–295 mOsm/kg)

  • Lower protein concentration than ICF (except plasma contains plasma proteins)

High-yield points:

Component ECF ICF
Na⁺ High Low
K⁺ Low High
Cl⁻ High Low
Protein Lower Higher
Osmolarity ≈290 mOsm/kg ≈290 mOsm/kg

Rapid Recall:
ECF = Na⁺ & Cl⁻ rich
ICF = K⁺ & Protein rich

Physiology.question: ৩) Thirst centre is stimulated by-?
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Intracellular dehydration. The thirst center in the hypothalamus is primarily stimulated by increased plasma osmolality, which causes water to move out of hypothalamic osmoreceptor cells, leading to intracellular dehydration and activation of thirst.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Decreased ECF tonicity – Decreases thirst by reducing osmoreceptor stimulation.

  • গ) Hypervolemia – Suppresses thirst; hypovolemia stimulates it.

  • ঘ) Angiotensin I – Angiotensin II, not Angiotensin I, stimulates the thirst center.

High-yield points:

  • Primary stimulus: ↑ Plasma osmolality → Intracellular dehydration of hypothalamic osmoreceptors

  • Secondary stimulus: ↓ Blood volume/↓ Blood pressure → Angiotensin II

  • Angiotensin II stimulates both thirst and ADH release.

  • ADH and thirst are regulated by the hypothalamus.

Rapid Recall:
Thirst = ↑ Osmolality + Intracellular dehydration + Angiotensin II + Hypovolemia

Physiology.question: ৪) Severe Hypotonicity of ECF compared to ICF may lead to-?
Physiology.exp:
Reference-Davidson/23rd/P-435/Fig-16.6

When the ECF becomes severely hypotonic relative to the ICF, water moves into cells by osmosis, causing cellular swelling (overhydration). In the brain, because the skull limits expansion, this results in cerebral oedema, the most serious and clinically important consequence.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Cellular overhydration – True, but cerebral oedema is the most significant clinical consequence and is the best answer.

  • গ) Cellular dehydration – Occurs with hypertonic ECF, not hypotonic ECF.

  • ঘ) Hyperkalemia – Not a direct consequence of hypotonic ECF.

High-yield points:

  • Hypotonic ECF → Water enters cells → Cell swelling

  • Brain is most vulnerable → Cerebral oedema

  • Hypertonic ECF → Water leaves cells → Cellular dehydration

  • Rapid hyponatremia is a common cause of cerebral oedema

Rapid Recall:

  • Hypotonic ECF → Cell swelling → Cerebral oedema

  • Hypertonic ECF → Cell shrinkage → Cellular dehydration

Physiology.question: ৫) Ptyalin is required in digestion of
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Carbohydrate.

Ptyalin (salivary α-amylase) is the principal enzyme in saliva. It initiates the digestion of starch (carbohydrate) by breaking α-1,4 glycosidic bonds to produce maltose, maltotriose, and dextrins. Its action is inactivated in the acidic environment of the stomach.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Protein – Digested by pepsin in the stomach and pancreatic proteases.

  • গ) Lipid – Mainly digested by pancreatic lipase (lingual and gastric lipases have minor roles).

  • ঘ) Minerals – Do not require enzymatic digestion.

High-yield points:

  • Ptyalin = Salivary α-amylase

  • Site of secretion: Salivary glands

  • Substrate: Starch (carbohydrate)

  • Products: Maltose, maltotriose, α-limit dextrins

  • Optimum pH: ~6.7–7.0

  • Inactivated by: Gastric acid

Rapid Recall:
Ptyalin = Saliva = Starch digestion.

Physiology.question: ৬) Substance that increase salivary secretion
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Histamine. Histamine can increase salivary secretion by promoting vasodilation and stimulating glandular secretion, although the physiological regulator of salivary secretion is parasympathetic (cholinergic) stimulation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Ergotamine – Has vasoconstrictor effects and does not increase salivary secretion.

  • গ) Atropine – Antimuscarinic drug that markedly reduces salivary secretion, causing dry mouth.

  • ঘ) Chloroform – General anesthetic; does not stimulate salivary secretion.

High-yield points:

  • Major stimulant of salivary secretion: Parasympathetic (Acetylcholine, M3 receptors)

  • Drugs increasing salivation: Pilocarpine, Bethanechol

  • Drug causing dry mouth (xerostomia): Atropine

  • Sympathetic stimulation: Produces a small volume of viscous, protein-rich saliva.

Physiology.question: ৭) Source of Pepsinogen
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Chief cell (zymogenic/peptic cell). Chief cells, located in the fundus and body of the stomach, secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) converts pepsinogen into active pepsin.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Parietal cell – Secretes HCl and intrinsic factor.

  • গ) G cell – Secretes gastrin.

  • ঘ) EC (enterochromaffin) cell – Secretes serotonin (5-HT). (Note: ECL cells secrete histamine.)

High-yield points:

Cell Secretion
Chief cell Pepsinogen
Parietal cell HCl, Intrinsic factor
G cell Gastrin
ECL cell Histamine
EC cell Serotonin (5-HT)

Rapid Recall:
Chief = Pepsinogen
Parietal = HCl + Intrinsic factor
G = Gastrin
ECL = Histamine

Physiology.question: ৮) Digestion of proteins starts in
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Stomach. Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where pepsin, activated from pepsinogen by hydrochloric acid (HCl), starts breaking proteins into smaller peptides.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Mouth – No protein-digesting enzyme is present.

  • গ) Small intestine – Protein digestion continues here with trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, and carboxypeptidases, but it does not begin here.

  • ঘ) Large intestine – No significant protein digestion occurs.

High-yield points:

  • Protein digestion starts: Stomach

  • Enzyme initiating digestion: Pepsin

  • Pepsinogen source: Chief cells

  • HCl source: Parietal cells

  • Protein digestion completed: Small intestine by pancreatic proteases and brush-border peptidases.

Rapid Recall:

  • Carbohydrate → Mouth (Ptyalin)

  • Protein → Stomach (Pepsin)

  • Fat → Small intestine (Pancreatic lipase)

Physiology.question: ৯) Increased pressure within the carotid sinus results in -
Physiology.option4: Decrease in diameter of blood vessels
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Reflex bradycardia.

Increased pressure in the carotid sinus stretches the baroreceptors, increasing their firing via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) to the medulla. This results in:

  • ↑ Parasympathetic (vagal) activity

  • ↓ Sympathetic activity

The net effect is bradycardia, vasodilation, and a fall in blood pressure.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Reflex hyperpnea – Carotid body chemoreceptors, not baroreceptors, influence respiration.

  • গ) Increase in sympathetic tone – Sympathetic tone decreases.

  • ঘ) Decrease in diameter of blood vessels – Baroreceptor activation causes vasodilation (increased vessel diameter), not vasoconstriction.

High-yield points:

  • Carotid sinus: Baroreceptor (pressure receptor)

  • Afferent nerve: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

  • Aortic arch baroreceptor afferent: Vagus nerve (CN X)

  • Increased BP → ↑ Baroreceptor firing → Bradycardia + Vasodilation + ↓ BP

Rapid Recall:

  • ↑ BP → ↑ Baroreceptor firing → ↓ Sympathetic + ↑ Vagal tone → Bradycardia

  • Carotid body = Chemoreceptor (O₂, CO₂, H⁺)

  • Carotid sinus = Baroreceptor (Blood pressure)

Physiology.question: ১০) Compensatory changes in hemorrhage include-
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Increase adrenal medullary secretions.

During hemorrhage, the fall in blood volume and blood pressure activates the baroreceptor reflex, leading to:

  • ↑ Sympathetic nervous activity

  • ↑ Adrenal medullary secretion of adrenaline and noradrenaline

  • Tachycardia

  • Peripheral vasoconstriction

  • Activation of the RAAS, producing angiotensin II (not angiotensin I as the major active compensatory hormone).

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Bradycardia – Hemorrhage causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.

  • গ) Decrease sympathetic nervous activity – Sympathetic activity increases.

  • ঘ) Increase circulating angiotensin-1 – Although angiotensin I is formed transiently, the physiologically important compensatory response is an increase in angiotensin II.

High-yield points:

  • Hemorrhage → ↓ BP → ↑ Sympathetic activity

  • ↑ Adrenaline & noradrenaline

  • ↑ Heart rate and contractility

  • Peripheral vasoconstriction

  • ↑ Renin → ↑ Angiotensin II → ↑ Aldosterone

  • ↑ ADH secretion

Rapid Recall:

Hemorrhage = "SNS + RAAS + ADH"

  • SNS → Tachycardia, vasoconstriction

  • RAAS → Angiotensin II, aldosterone

  • ADH → Water retention

Physiology.question: ১১) Heart rate is accelerated by
Physiology.exp:
Exercise increases heart rate by:

  • ↑ Sympathetic stimulation

  • ↓ Vagal (parasympathetic) tone

  • Increased circulating adrenaline

Fear can also cause tachycardia through sympathetic activation, but in single-best-answer physiology questions, exercise is the classic physiological stimulus.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • গ) Increased baroreceptor activity → Reflex bradycardia (↑ vagal tone, ↓ sympathetic tone)

  • ঘ) Increased intracranial pressure → Reflex bradycardia (Cushing reflex)

High-yield points:

  • Exercise → Tachycardia

  • Fear/anxiety → Tachycardia

  • ↑ Baroreceptor activity → Bradycardia

  • ↑ Intracranial pressure → Bradycardia (Cushing reflex)

Rapid Recall:

  • Exercise, fear, fever, hyperthyroidism → ↑ Heart rate

  • Baroreceptor stimulation, carotid sinus massage, raised ICP → ↓ Heart rate

Physiology.question: ১২) Total peripheral resistance is inversely proportional to
Physiology.option3: Cross sectional area of blood vessels
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Cross-sectional area of blood vessels.

According to Poiseuille's law:

R∝ηLr4R∝r4ηL​​

where:

  • R = Resistance

  • η = Blood viscosity

  • L = Vessel length

  • r = Vessel radius

Thus:

  • Resistance increases with blood viscosity and vessel length.

  • Resistance decreases as vessel radius (and therefore cross-sectional area) increases.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Velocity of blood flow – Not directly inversely proportional to total peripheral resistance.

  • খ) Viscosity of blood – Resistance is directly proportional.

  • ঘ) Length of blood vessels – Resistance is directly proportional.

High-yield points:

  • TPR ∝ Viscosity

  • TPR ∝ Vessel length

  • TPR ∝ 1/r⁴ (radius is the most important determinant)

  • Arterioles are the major resistance vessels.

Rapid Recall:

  • ↑ Radius → ↓ Resistance

  • ↑ Viscosity → ↑ Resistance

  • ↑ Length → ↑ Resistance

  • Arterioles determine Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR)

Physiology.question: ১৩) Following cardiovascular changes occurs after birth –
Physiology.option1: Decrease in the system vascular resistance
Physiology.exp:
The correct answer is Closure of ductus venosus.

After birth, several important cardiovascular changes occur:

  • Closure of ductus venosus after the umbilical cord is clamped.

  • ↑ Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) due to loss of the low-resistance placental circulation.

  • ↓ Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) because lung expansion increases oxygenation.

  • ↓ Right ventricular pressure and ↑ Left ventricular pressure.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Decrease in systemic vascular resistance – Incorrect; SVR increases.

  • খ) Pulmonary arterial constriction – Incorrect; pulmonary arteries dilate.

  • গ) Increase in right ventricular pressure – Incorrect; right ventricular pressure decreases.

High-yield points:

  • Cord clamping → ↑ SVR

  • First breath → ↓ PVR

  • Foramen ovale closes (functional)

  • Ductus arteriosus closes

  • Ductus venosus closes

Rapid Recall:

  • SVR ↑

  • PVR ↓

  • RV pressure ↓

  • LV pressure ↑

  • FO, DA, DV close

Physiology.question: ১৪) Increased vagal tone tends to increase
Physiology.exp:
The vagus nerve (parasympathetic) stimulates the gastrointestinal tract, leading to:

  • ↑ Gastric HCl secretion

  • ↑ Gastric motility and peristalsis

  • ↑ Digestive gland secretion

  • ↓ Heart rate

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Heart rate – Decreases (vagal stimulation causes bradycardia).

  • খ) Decreased peristalsis – Incorrect; vagal stimulation increases peristalsis.

  • গ) Diameter of blood vessel – Parasympathetic innervation to most blood vessels is minimal; it is not a general effect of increased vagal tone.

High-yield points:

  • Vagus = "Rest and Digest"

  • Heart: ↓ Heart rate

  • GIT: ↑ Peristalsis, ↑ HCl secretion, ↑ Digestive secretions

  • Bronchi: Bronchoconstriction

  • Pupil: Miosis

Rapid Recall:

  • Sympathetic: Fight or Flight → ↑ HR, ↓ GIT activity

  • Parasympathetic (Vagus): Rest and Digest → ↓ HR, ↑ Peristalsis, ↑ HCl secretion

Physiology.question: ১৫) The pulse pressure in the large arteries is directly proportional to
Physiology.exp:
Pulse pressure (PP) is the difference between systolic BP and diastolic BP.

Pulse Pressure∝Stroke VolumeArterial CompliancePulse Pressure∝Arterial ComplianceStroke Volume​​

Therefore:

  • ↑ Stroke volume → ↑ Pulse pressure (direct relationship)

  • ↑ Arterial compliance → ↓ Pulse pressure (inverse relationship)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Heart rate – No direct proportional relationship with pulse pressure.

  • গ) Total peripheral resistance – Mainly affects diastolic pressure, not pulse pressure directly.

  • ঘ) Compliance of arterial wall – Pulse pressure is inversely, not directly, proportional to compliance.

High-yield points:

  • PP = SBP − DBP

  • ↑ Stroke volume → ↑ PP

  • ↓ Arterial compliance (aging, atherosclerosis) → ↑ PP

  • Aortic regurgitation → Wide PP

  • Aortic stenosis, shock → Narrow PP

Rapid Recall:

  • Pulse Pressure ∝ Stroke Volume

  • Pulse Pressure ∝ 1 / Arterial Compliance

Physiology.question: ১৬) Cardiac muscle fibers-
Physiology.option2: Have a T - system of tubules between the A and I band
Physiology.option3: Have intercalated discs where there are desmosomes and gap (communicating) Junctions
Physiology.exp:
The characteristic feature of cardiac muscle is the presence of intercalated discs, which contain:

  • Desmosomes (macula adherens) → Mechanical attachment

  • Gap junctions → Electrical coupling, allowing rapid spread of action potentials

This enables the heart to function as a functional syncytium.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Have a peripheral nucleus – Incorrect; cardiac muscle cells have one (occasionally two) centrally located nucleus.

  • খ) Have a T-system of tubules between the A and I band – Incorrect; cardiac muscle T-tubules are located at the Z line (junction of A and I bands), not "between the A and I band" as stated.

  • ঘ) Have motor end plates – Incorrect; cardiac muscle does not have motor end plates. It is myogenic and is modulated by the autonomic nervous system.

High-yield points:

  • Central nucleus

  • Branching fibers

  • Intercalated discs = Desmosomes + Gap junctions

  • T-tubules at Z line (A–I junction)

  • No motor end plates

Rapid Recall:

Muscle Nucleus T-tubule Motor end plate
Skeletal Peripheral A–I junction Present
Cardiac Central Z line (A–I junction) Absent
Smooth Central No T-tubules Absent

Physiology.question: ১৭) Food intake is regulated by
Physiology.exp:
The hypothalamus regulates food intake by integrating peripheral signals, the most important long-term signal being leptin, a hormone secreted by adipose tissue.

  • ↑ Leptin → ↓ Appetite (stimulates satiety center, inhibits hunger center)

  • ↓ Leptin → ↑ Appetite

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Thermostatic mechanism – An old theory; not the principal regulator of food intake.

  • গ) Specific dynamic action (thermic effect) of food – Increases energy expenditure after meals but does not regulate appetite directly.

  • ঘ) Basal metabolic rate (BMR) – Determines resting energy expenditure, not the primary control of food intake.

High-yield points:

  • Leptin → Adipocytes → ↓ Appetite

  • Ghrelin → Stomach → ↑ Appetite

  • NPY/AgRP neurons → Stimulate feeding

  • POMC/CART neurons → Suppress feeding

Rapid Recall:

  • Leptin = Satiety hormone

  • Ghrelin = Hunger hormone

  • Hypothalamus = Feeding center (lateral) + Satiety center (ventromedial)

Physiology.question: ১৮) Which of the following has the highest pH?
Physiology.exp:
Pancreatic juice has the highest pH (≈ 8.0–8.3) because it contains a high concentration of bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) secreted by pancreatic ductal cells. This neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum.

Approximate pH values:

  • Gastric juice: 1–3 (most acidic)

  • Saliva: 6.2–7.6

  • Colonic luminal contents: 5.5–7.0 (slightly acidic due to bacterial fermentation)

  • Pancreatic juice: 8.0–8.3 (most alkaline)

High-yield points:

  • Highest pH: Pancreatic juice

  • Lowest pH: Gastric juice

  • Secretin → ↑ Pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion

  • CCK → ↑ Pancreatic enzyme secretion

Rapid Recall:

Fluid Approximate pH
Gastric juice 1–3
Saliva 6.2–7.6
Colonic contents 5.5–7.0
Pancreatic juice 8.0–8.3

Physiology.question: ১৯) In infants, defecation often follows a meal. The cause of colonic contractions in this situation is -?
Physiology.exp:
In infants, feeding commonly triggers colonic mass movements and defecation due to the gastrocolic reflex.

  • Food entering the stomach → Gastric distension

  • Activation of vagal and enteric neural reflexes

  • Increased colonic motility (mass movements)

  • Defecation shortly after feeding

This reflex is particularly strong in infants, explaining why they often pass stool soon after a meal.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Histamine – Stimulates gastric acid secretion, not colonic contractions.

  • খ) Increased circulating levels of CCK – Stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion, not the primary cause of postprandial defecation.

  • ঘ) Increased circulating levels of somatostatin – Inhibits GI secretion and motility.

High-yield points:

  • Gastrocolic reflex: Stomach distension → ↑ Colonic mass movements

  • Most prominent in infants

  • Helps empty the colon after meals

Rapid Recall:

  • Gastrocolic reflex → Stomach → Colon

  • Enterogastric reflex → Duodenum → Stomach (inhibits gastric emptying)

  • Rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR) → Rectal distension → Internal anal sphincter relaxation

Physiology.question: ২০) The migrating motor complex is triggered by which of the following?
Physiology.exp:
The Migrating Motor Complex (MMC) is a cyclic pattern of gastrointestinal motility that occurs during the fasting (interdigestive) state, approximately every 90–120 minutes.

It is triggered by motilin, a hormone secreted by M cells of the duodenum and jejunum.

Functions of MMC:

  • Sweeps residual food from the stomach and small intestine

  • Prevents bacterial overgrowth

  • Called the "intestinal housekeeper"

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) NO (Nitric oxide) – Mediates smooth muscle relaxation, not MMC initiation.

  • গ) CCK – Released after meals; stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion, and suppresses MMC.

  • ঘ) Somatostatin – Inhibits GI secretion and motility; does not trigger MMC.

High-yield points:

  • Motilin → MMC

  • Occurs during fasting

  • Interval: Every 90–120 minutes

  • Feeding abolishes MMC

  • Erythromycin is a motilin receptor agonist and can stimulate MMC (used as a prokinetic).

Rapid Recall:

  • Motilin = Migrating Motor Complex

  • Fasting = MMC ON

  • Feeding = MMC OFF

Physiology.question: ২১) Which of the following hormones acts on its target tissues by a steroid hormone mechanism of action?
Physiology.option3: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) on the collecting duct
Physiology.exp:
Although thyroid hormone (T₃/T₄) is derived from the amino acid tyrosine, it acts by a steroid hormone-like mechanism.

  • Enters the cell (T₄ is converted to T₃)

  • T₃ binds to nuclear thyroid hormone receptors

  • Alters gene transcription → changes protein synthesis

  • Slow onset, prolonged action

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Parathyroid hormone (PTH) – Acts via G-protein-coupled receptor (Gs → cAMP).

  • গ) ADH on the collecting duct (V₂ receptor) – Acts via Gs → cAMP → insertion of aquaporin-2 channels.

  • ঘ) β₁-adrenergic agonists – Act via Gs-coupled receptors → ↑ cAMP.

High-yield points:

Hormones acting via intracellular (nuclear) receptors:

  • Thyroid hormone (T₃/T₄)

  • Cortisol

  • Aldosterone

  • Estrogen

  • Progesterone

  • Testosterone

  • Calcitriol (Vitamin D)

Rapid Recall:

  • Steroid-like mechanism: Thyroid hormone + Steroid hormones + Vitamin D

  • PTH, ADH (V₂), β₁ agonists: GPCR → cAMP

Physiology.question: ২২) Which of the following hormones originates in the anterior pituitary?
Physiology.exp:
TSH is synthesized and secreted by thyrotroph cells of the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis). It stimulates the thyroid gland to produce T₃ and T₄.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) – Secreted by the hypothalamus.

  • খ) Somatostatin – Secreted by the hypothalamus (also by pancreatic δ cells and GI tract).

  • গ) Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) – Secreted by the hypothalamus.

High-yield points:

Anterior pituitary hormones (FLAT PEG):

  • FSH

  • LH

  • ACTH

  • TSH

  • Prolactin

  • Endorphins (minor)

  • Growth hormone

Rapid Recall:

  • Hypothalamus: GHRH, GnRH, TRH, CRH, Somatostatin, Dopamine

  • Anterior pituitary: TSH, ACTH, GH, FSH, LH, Prolactin

Physiology.question: ২৩) Which of the following inhibits the secretion of growth hormone by the anterior pituitary?
Physiology.exp:
Somatomedins (mainly IGF-1) are produced by the liver in response to growth hormone (GH). They exert negative feedback by:

  • Directly inhibiting GH secretion from the anterior pituitary.

  • Stimulating hypothalamic somatostatin, which further suppresses GH release.

The other options are incorrect because they increase GH secretion:

  • ক) Sleep – Especially deep (slow-wave) sleep increases GH release.

  • খ) Stress – Physical stress, exercise, trauma, and hypoglycemia stimulate GH secretion.

  • গ) Puberty – Sex steroids increase GH secretion, producing the pubertal growth spurt.

High-yield points:

Stimulators of GH:

  • GHRH

  • Sleep

  • Exercise

  • Stress

  • Hypoglycemia

  • Puberty (estrogen/testosterone)

  • Ghrelin

Inhibitors of GH:

  • Somatostatin

  • IGF-1 (Somatomedin C)

  • Hyperglycemia

  • Elevated free fatty acids

Rapid Recall:

  • GHRH → ↑ GH

  • Somatostatin → ↓ GH

  • IGF-1 (Somatomedin C) → Negative feedback → ↓ GH

Physiology.question: ২৪) Selective destruction of the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex would produce a deficiency of which hormone?
Physiology.exp:
The zona glomerulosa is the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex and is responsible for the synthesis of aldosterone, the principal mineralocorticoid.

Adrenal cortex layers ("GFR – Salt, Sugar, Sex"):

  • Glomerulosa → Salt → Aldosterone

  • Fasciculata → Sugar → Cortisol

  • Reticularis → Sex → Androgens (DHEA, androstenedione)

Therefore, selective destruction of the zona glomerulosa causes aldosterone deficiency only.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Androstenedione – Produced mainly by the zona reticularis.

  • গ) Cortisol – Produced by the zona fasciculata.

  • ঘ) Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) – Produced by the zona reticularis.

High-yield points:

  • Zona glomerulosa → Aldosterone → Controlled mainly by Angiotensin II and K⁺

  • Zona fasciculata → Cortisol → Controlled by ACTH

  • Zona reticularis → DHEA, Androstenedione → Controlled by ACTH

Rapid Recall:

GFR = Salt, Sugar, Sex

  • Glomerulosa → Aldosterone

  • Fasciculata → Cortisol

  • Reticularis → Androgens (DHEA, Androstenedione)

Physiology.question: ২৫) Site of blood cell production at late fetal life
Physiology.exp:
The sites of hematopoiesis change during fetal development:

  • Yolk sac: 3 weeks – 3 months (early embryo)

  • Liver: 2–7 months (major fetal hematopoietic organ)

  • Spleen: 3–7 months

  • Red bone marrow: From 5th month onward and becomes the predominant site during late fetal life and after birth.

Therefore, in late fetal life, the main site of blood cell production is red bone marrow.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Yolk sac – Earliest embryonic hematopoiesis only.

  • খ) Liver – Major site in mid-fetal life, but not the principal site in late fetal life.

  • গ) Thymus – Site of T-lymphocyte maturation, not general hematopoiesis.

High-yield points:

Sequence of hematopoiesis:

  • Yolk sac → Liver → Spleen → Bone marrow

Rapid Recall:

  • Embryo: Yolk sac

  • Mid-fetus: Liver (± Spleen)

  • Late fetus & After birth: Red bone marrow

Physiology.question: ২৬) Sky rise of ESR is found in
Physiology.exp:
A markedly elevated ("sky-high") ESR is classically seen in multiple myeloma due to increased monoclonal immunoglobulins (paraproteins), which promote rouleaux formation of red blood cells, causing rapid sedimentation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Polycythaemia vera – ESR is low due to increased red cell mass.

  • খ) Pregnancy – ESR is moderately increased because of increased fibrinogen, but not typically "sky-high."

  • ঘ) Myocardial infarction (MI) – ESR may rise after 24–48 hours but is not usually markedly elevated.

High-yield points:

Markedly increased ESR:

  • Multiple myeloma

  • Waldenström macroglobulinaemia

  • Giant cell arteritis

  • Polymyalgia rheumatica

  • Severe infections (e.g., tuberculosis)

Low ESR:

  • Polycythaemia vera

  • Sickle cell disease

  • Hereditary spherocytosis

Rapid Recall:

  • "Sky-high ESR" → Think Multiple Myeloma

  • Polycythaemia vera → Low ESR

Physiology.question: ২৭) Which acts as microtubule-organizing centre?
Physiology.exp:
The centrosome is the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) of animal cells. It consists of two centrioles surrounded by pericentriolar material (PCM) containing γ-tubulin, which nucleates and organizes microtubules. It also forms the mitotic spindle during cell division.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Peroxisome – Involved in fatty acid oxidation and detoxification of hydrogen peroxide.

  • গ) Lysosome – Contains hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion.

  • ঘ) Ribosome – Site of protein synthesis.

High-yield points:

  • Centrosome = MTOC (Microtubule-Organizing Center)

  • Composed of 2 centrioles + pericentriolar material

  • Organizes the mitotic spindle during mitosis

Rapid Recall:

  • Centrosome → Microtubules

  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis

  • Lysosome → Intracellular digestion

  • Peroxisome → β-oxidation & H₂O₂ detoxification

Physiology.question: ২৮) Most prevalent plasma protein
Physiology.exp:
Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein, accounting for approximately 55–60% of total plasma proteins. It is synthesized by the liver.

Major functions of albumin:

  • Maintains plasma colloid (oncotic) pressure

  • Transports bilirubin, fatty acids, calcium, hormones, and drugs

  • Acts as a buffer for plasma pH

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Globulin – Makes up about 35–38% of plasma proteins.

  • গ) Fibrinogen – About 4–7%; involved in blood coagulation.

  • ঘ) Prothrombin – A clotting factor present in much smaller amounts.

High-yield points:

Approximate plasma protein distribution:

  • Albumin: 55–60%

  • Globulins: 35–38%

  • Fibrinogen: 4–7%

Rapid Recall:

  • Most abundant plasma protein → Albumin

  • Most abundant immunoglobulin → IgG

  • Most abundant intracellular cation → K⁺

  • Most abundant extracellular cation → Na⁺

Physiology.question: ২৯) Cell membrane is semipermeable because of having
Physiology.exp:
The cell membrane is selectively (semi-) permeable primarily because of its phospholipid bilayer. The hydrophobic lipid core acts as a barrier, allowing lipid-soluble molecules to diffuse easily while restricting the passage of water-soluble molecules and ions unless they pass through specific protein channels or carriers.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Protein – Membrane proteins facilitate transport but do not create the semipermeable barrier.

  • গ) Carbohydrate – Involved mainly in cell recognition and adhesion.

  • ঘ) Glycolipid – Functions in cell recognition and membrane stability, not semipermeability.

High-yield points:

  • Phospholipid bilayer → Selective permeability

  • Proteins → Channels, carriers, receptors

  • Carbohydrates → Glycocalyx (cell recognition)

  • Cholesterol → Regulates membrane fluidity

Rapid Recall:

  • Lipid → Semipermeable barrier

  • Protein → Transport & receptors

  • Carbohydrate → Cell recognition

  • Cholesterol → Membrane stability/fluidity

Physiology.question: ৩০) Which organelle is important in specialized cellular signalling?
Physiology.exp:
The endoplasmic reticulum (ER), particularly the smooth ER, plays a central role in specialized cellular signalling by acting as the major intracellular calcium (Ca²⁺) store. Release and reuptake of Ca²⁺ from the ER regulate numerous cellular processes, including muscle contraction, secretion, metabolism, gene expression, and apoptosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Golgi apparatus – Modifies, sorts, and packages proteins.

  • গ) Ribosome – Site of protein synthesis.

  • ঘ) Mitochondria – Primarily responsible for ATP production; also participates in apoptosis and calcium buffering but is not the principal organelle for specialized cellular signalling.

High-yield points:

  • Endoplasmic reticulum → Ca²⁺ storage & intracellular signalling

  • Golgi apparatus → Protein modification and packaging

  • Ribosomes → Protein synthesis

  • Mitochondria → ATP production ("powerhouse")

Rapid Recall:

  • ER → Calcium signalling

  • Golgi → Packaging

  • Ribosome → Protein synthesis

  • Mitochondria → ATP

Physiology.question: ৩১) Which of the following decreases the conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol?
Physiology.exp:
The conversion of 25-hydroxycholecalciferol [25(OH)D] to the active form 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol) occurs in the proximal tubules of the kidney by the enzyme 1α-hydroxylase.

In chronic renal failure (CKD):

  • Loss of functioning renal tissue → ↓ 1α-hydroxylase activity

  • ↓ Conversion of 25(OH)D → 1,25(OH)₂D (calcitriol)

  • Leads to hypocalcemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism

The other options are incorrect because they stimulate 1α-hydroxylase:

  • ক) Hypocalcemia → ↑ PTH → ↑ calcitriol synthesis

  • খ) Hyperparathyroidism → PTH stimulates 1α-hydroxylase

  • গ) Hypophosphatemia → Directly stimulates 1α-hydroxylase

High-yield points:

Stimulators of 1α-hydroxylase:

  • PTH

  • Hypocalcemia (via PTH)

  • Hypophosphatemia

Inhibitors:

  • Chronic kidney disease

  • Hyperphosphatemia

  • FGF-23

Rapid Recall:

  • Liver: Vitamin D → 25(OH)D

  • Kidney (1α-hydroxylase): 25(OH)D → 1,25(OH)₂D (Calcitriol)

  • CKD → ↓ Calcitriol production

Physiology.question: ৩২) Which of the following causes increased aldosterone secretion?
Physiology.option2: Administration of an inhibitor of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
Physiology.exp:
A decrease in blood volume activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS):

  • ↓ Blood volume/↓ renal perfusion

  • ↑ Renin release

  • ↑ Angiotensin II

  • ↑ Aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) ACE inhibitor – ↓ Angiotensin II → ↓ Aldosterone

  • গ) Hyperosmolarity – Stimulates ADH, not aldosterone.

  • ঘ) Hypokalemia – Suppresses aldosterone secretion (whereas hyperkalemia stimulates it).

High-yield points:

Stimulators of aldosterone:

  • ↓ Blood volume / ↓ Blood pressure

  • Angiotensin II

  • Hyperkalemia

Inhibitors of aldosterone:

  • ACE inhibitors

  • ANP (Atrial natriuretic peptide)

  • Hypokalemia

Rapid Recall:

  • ↓ Blood volume → ↑ Renin → ↑ Angiotensin II → ↑ Aldosterone

  • Hyperkalemia → ↑ Aldosterone

  • ACE inhibitors → ↓ Aldosterone

Physiology.question: ৩৩) Secretion of oxytocin is increased by-?
Physiology.exp:
Oxytocin is synthesized in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. Its secretion is increased by stretching (dilation) of the cervix, producing the Ferguson reflex, a classic positive feedback mechanism during labor.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Milk ejection – Occurs as a result of oxytocin release. The physiological stimulus is suckling, not milk ejection itself.

  • গ) Increased prolactin levels – Prolactin stimulates milk production, not oxytocin secretion.

  • ঘ) Increased ECF volume – Has no role in regulating oxytocin secretion.

High-yield points:

Stimuli for oxytocin release:

  • Cervical dilation (Ferguson reflex)

  • Suckling of the nipple

Actions of oxytocin:

  • Uterine contractions

  • Milk ejection (let-down reflex)

Rapid Recall:

  • Oxytocin = Milk ejection + Uterine contraction

  • Prolactin = Milk production

  • Ferguson reflex → Cervical dilation → ↑ Oxytocin

Physiology.question: ৩৪) Contraction of medial rectus helps in accommodation of eye by
৩৫) Post ganglionic neurotransmitter of sympathetic division
৩৬) Most important characteristic of synaptic transmission-
Physiology.exp:
The most important characteristic of chemical synaptic transmission is one-way (unidirectional) conduction.

Presynaptic terminalSynaptic cleftPostsynaptic cell
Synapse is ready
The sending cell has neurotransmitter ready to release.
Move through the stages to trace how an electrical signal becomes a chemical signal and then a local electrical response.

Transmission occurs only from:

  • Presynaptic neuron → Synaptic cleft → Postsynaptic neuron

This is because:

  • Neurotransmitters are released only from the presynaptic terminal.

  • Receptors for these neurotransmitters are present only on the postsynaptic membrane.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Excitation – Synapses can be excitatory or inhibitory.

  • খ) Synaptic delay – A characteristic (~0.5 ms), but not the most important.

  • গ) Summation – Important property of neuronal integration but not the defining characteristic.

High-yield points:

  • Most important property → One-way conduction

  • Synaptic delay ≈ 0.5 ms

  • Synapses may be excitatory or inhibitory

  • Temporal and spatial summation occur at synapses

Rapid Recall:

  • Chemical synapse → Unidirectional

  • Electrical synapse → Usually bidirectional

  • Reason: Neurotransmitter release is presynaptic; receptors are postsynaptic

Physiology.question: ৩৭) Neurotransmitter of Fast pain-
Physiology.exp:
Fast pain is transmitted by Aδ (A-delta) fibers, which primarily release glutamate as their neurotransmitter.

  • Glutamate mediates fast, sharp, well-localized pain.

  • Substance P is mainly associated with slow, dull, burning pain transmitted by C fibers.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • খ) Substance P – Neurotransmitter of slow pain, not fast pain.

  • গ) Serotonin – Modulates pain pathways but is not the primary neurotransmitter of fast pain.

  • ঘ) Acetylcholine – Not involved in primary pain transmission.

High-yield points:

  • Fast pain → Aδ fibers → Glutamate

  • Slow pain → C fibers → Substance P (± glutamate)

Rapid Recall:

  • Aδ = Acute = Glutamate

  • C fibers = Chronic = Substance P

Physiology.question: ৩৮) Paralysis of lower half of the body
৩৯) Which is substrate for Lysosomal enzyme cathepsins?
Physiology.exp:
Reference: Ganong 26th; Table-2.1

Cathepsins are the major lysosomal proteolytic enzymes (proteases). Their principal substrate is protein, which they degrade into peptides and amino acids within the acidic environment of lysosomes.

The other options are incorrect:

  • ক) DNA – Degraded by DNase.

  • খ) RNA – Degraded by RNase.

  • ঘ) Collagen – Although cathepsin K can degrade collagen, collagen is a specific protein. Since the question asks about the substrate of cathepsins in general, the best answer is protein.

High-Yield Points:

Lysosomal Enzyme Main Substrate
Cathepsins Protein
DNase DNA
RNase RNA
Lipase Lipids
Glycosidases Carbohydrates
Phosphatases Phosphate esters

Rapid Recall:

  • Cathepsins = Proteases = Protein

  • DNase → DNA

  • RNase → RNA

  • Lysosome = Intracellular digestion

Physiology.question: ৪০) Which of the following pancreatic secretions has a receptor with four subunits, two of which have tyrosine kinase activity?
Physiology.exp:
The insulin receptor is a tetrameric receptor composed of four subunits (α₂β₂):

  • 2 α (alpha) subunits – extracellular, bind insulin.

  • 2 β (beta) subunits – transmembrane and possess intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity.

When insulin binds to the α-subunits, the β-subunits undergo autophosphorylation, activating intracellular signaling pathways (e.g., PI3K/Akt pathway), leading to GLUT-4 translocation and metabolic effects.

The other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Glucagon – Acts via a G protein-coupled receptor (Gs) → ↑ cAMP.

  • গ) Somatostatin – Acts via a Gi-coupled GPCR → ↓ cAMP.

  • ঘ) Pancreatic lipase – An enzyme, not a hormone; it has no receptor.

High-Yield Receptor Table

Hormone Receptor Type
Insulin Tyrosine kinase receptor (α₂β₂)
Glucagon Gs-coupled GPCR
Somatostatin Gi-coupled GPCR
Pancreatic lipase Enzyme (no receptor)

Rapid Recall

  • Insulin → Tyrosine kinase receptor

  • Glucagon → Gs → ↑ cAMP

  • Somatostatin → Gi → ↓ cAMP

  • Insulin receptor = α₂β₂ (4 subunits)

Physiology.question: ৪১) Which of the following substances is released from neurons in the GI tract and produces smooth muscle relaxation?
Physiology.exp:
Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) is a neurocrine released from neurons of the enteric nervous system. It causes:

  • Relaxation of gastrointestinal smooth muscle (including GI sphincters)

  • Vasodilation

  • Increased intestinal and pancreatic fluid secretion

  • Inhibition of gastric acid secretion

The other options are incorrect because they are endocrine hormones secreted by enteroendocrine cells, not neurotransmitters from enteric neurons:

  • ক) Secretin – Secreted by S cells of the duodenum; stimulates pancreatic HCO₃⁻ secretion.

  • খ) Gastrin – Secreted by G cells; stimulates gastric acid secretion.

  • গ) Cholecystokinin (CCK) – Secreted by I cells; stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.

High-Yield Points

Substance Source Major Action
VIP Enteric neurons Smooth muscle relaxation, ↑ intestinal secretion, vasodilation
Secretin S cells ↑ HCO₃⁻ secretion
Gastrin G cells ↑ Gastric acid secretion
CCK I cells ↑ Pancreatic enzymes, gallbladder contraction

Rapid Recall

  • VIP = Neuron = Smooth muscle relaxation

  • Gastrin = Acid

  • Secretin = Bicarbonate

  • CCK = Enzymes + Gallbladder contraction

Physiology.question: ৪২) Which of the following is the site of Na+–bile acid cotransport?
Physiology.exp:
The terminal ileum is the primary site of Na⁺–bile acid cotransport via the Apical Sodium-dependent Bile Acid Transporter (ASBT). This process is a key part of the enterohepatic circulation, allowing about 95% of bile acids to be reabsorbed and returned to the liver.

The other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Gastric antrum – Involved in gastrin secretion, not bile acid absorption.

  • খ) Gastric fundus – Mainly stores food and secretes acid and intrinsic factor.

  • গ) Duodenum – Site of bile acid action in fat digestion, not the major site of bile acid reabsorption.

High-Yield Points

Site Major Function
Terminal ileum Na⁺–bile acid cotransport (ASBT), Vitamin B₁₂ absorption
Duodenum Iron absorption
Jejunum Major nutrient absorption
Colon Water and electrolyte absorption

Rapid Recall

  • Terminal ileum = Bile salts + Vitamin B₁₂

  • Duodenum = Iron

  • Jejunum = Most nutrients

  • Colon = Water

Physiology.question: ৪৩) Following which is most important control system under negative feedback mechanism-?
Physiology.exp:
Negative feedback is the principal mechanism for maintaining homeostasis. Among the options, regulation of body water balance is one of the most important examples of a negative feedback control system.

  • An increase in plasma osmolality stimulates ADH (vasopressin) release.

  • ADH increases water reabsorption in the kidneys.

  • Plasma osmolality then returns to normal, reducing further ADH secretion.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Blood clotting – Positive feedback.

  • খ) LH surge – Positive feedback (estrogen stimulates further LH release before ovulation).

  • ঘ) Blood pressure control system – Also a negative feedback system (baroreceptor reflex), but in standard physiology texts (e.g., Guyton), water balance regulation is considered a classic and especially important example of homeostatic negative feedback.

High-Yield Points

Process Feedback Type
Regulation of water balance (ADH) Negative
Blood pressure (baroreceptor reflex) Negative
Blood clotting Positive
LH surge Positive
Parturition (oxytocin) Positive

Physiology.question: ৪৪) The Golgi complex-
Physiology.option1: is an organelle that participates in the breakdown of proteins and lipids.
Physiology.option2: is an organelle that participates in posttranslational processing of proteins.
Physiology.option3: is an organelle that participates in energy production.
Physiology.option4: is an organelle that participates in transcription and translation.
Physiology.exp:
The Golgi apparatus (Golgi complex) is responsible for the post-translational modification, sorting, packaging, and secretion of proteins received from the rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER). It also forms lysosomes and secretory vesicles.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ক) Breakdown of proteins and lipids – This is the function of lysosomes, not the Golgi apparatus.

  • গ) Energy production – This is the function of mitochondria.

  • ঘ) Transcription and translation – Transcription occurs in the nucleus, while translation occurs on ribosomes (especially on the rough ER).

High-Yield Organelle Functions

Organelle Main Function
Golgi apparatus Post-translational modification, sorting, packaging
Rough ER Protein synthesis
Smooth ER Lipid synthesis, detoxification, Ca²⁺ storage
Lysosome Intracellular digestion
Mitochondria ATP production
Ribosome Translation
Nucleus Transcription

Rapid Recall

  • Golgi = Modify + Package + Sort + Secrete

  • RER = Protein synthesis

  • SER = Lipid synthesis

  • Lysosome = Digestion

  • Mitochondria = ATP

Physiology.question: ৪৫) Ovulation occurs at day
৪৬) Lesion of left optic radiation results in
৪৭) Krause end bulb
৪৮) Which one is concerned with converting recent memory to long term memory?
Physiology.exp:
The hippocampus is the brain structure primarily responsible for memory consolidation—the conversion of recent (short-term) memory into long-term memory. Bilateral hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia, in which new long-term memories cannot be formed.

The other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Amygdala – Involved in emotional processing and emotional memory (especially fear).

  • গ) Putamen – Part of the basal ganglia, involved in motor control and procedural learning.

  • ঘ) Pallidum (Globus pallidus) – Also part of the basal ganglia, involved in regulation of movement.

High-Yield Functions

Structure Main Function
Hippocampus Consolidation of short-term to long-term memory
Amygdala Emotion, fear, emotional memory
Putamen Motor control, procedural learning
Globus pallidus Motor regulation

Rapid Recall

  • Hippocampus = Memory formation & consolidation

  • Amygdala = Emotion (fear)

  • Basal ganglia (Putamen + Pallidum) = Movement

  • Bilateral hippocampal lesion → Anterograde amnesia

Physiology.question: ৪৯) Which of the following would occur as a result of the inhibition of Na+,K+-ATPase?
Physiology.exp:
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ into the cell, maintaining a low intracellular Na⁺ concentration.

When the pump is inhibited (e.g., by digoxin):

  • Intracellular Na⁺ increases.

  • The Na⁺ gradient decreases.

  • Activity of the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX) decreases, so less Ca²⁺ is extruded.

  • Intracellular Ca²⁺ increases, enhancing cardiac contractility.

High-Yield Points

Effect of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition Result
Intracellular Na⁺ ↑
Intracellular K⁺ ↓
Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger activity ↓
Intracellular Ca²⁺ ↑
Na⁺-dependent glucose uptake ↓

Rapid Recall

  • Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition → ↑ Na⁺ inside → ↓ Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange → ↑ Ca²⁺ inside.

  • Digoxin works by inhibiting Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → Positive inotropic effect.

Physiology.question: ৫০) Which of the following substances or combinations of substances could be used to measure interstitial fluid volume?
Physiology.exp:
nterstitial fluid (ISF) volume cannot be measured directly. It is calculated as:

Interstitial fluid volume = Extracellular fluid (ECF) volume − Plasma volume

Therefore:

  • Inulin measures ECF volume (distributes throughout extracellular fluid but does not enter cells).

  • Radioactive albumin measures plasma volume (albumin remains within the vascular compartment).

Subtracting plasma volume from ECF volume gives the interstitial fluid volume.

High-Yield Fluid Compartments

Marker Measures
D₂O, ³H₂O, antipyrine Total body water (TBW)
Inulin, Mannitol, Sucrose Extracellular fluid (ECF)
Evans blue, Radioactive albumin Plasma volume
Interstitial fluid ECF − Plasma volume
Intracellular fluid TBW − ECF

Rapid Recall

  • TBW → D₂O

  • ECF → Inulin

  • Plasma → Evans blue / Radioactive albumin

  • ISF = Inulin − Radioactive albumin

Physiology.question: ৫১) Erythropoietin is secreted by-?
Physiology.option3: granular cells in the juxtaglomerular apparatus.
Physiology.option4: Cells in the peritubular capillary bed.
Physiology.exp:
Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced primarily by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells located around the peritubular capillaries in the renal cortex and outer medulla. These cells respond to hypoxia by increasing EPO secretion, which stimulates erythropoiesis in the bone marrow.

High-Yield Points

Structure Hormone Secreted
Peritubular interstitial cells Erythropoietin (EPO)
Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells Renin
Macula densa Senses NaCl; regulates renin release

Rapid Recall

  • EPO → Peritubular interstitial fibroblasts (kidney)

  • Renin → Juxtaglomerular cells

  • Hypoxia → ↑ EPO → ↑ RBC production

Physiology.question: ৫২) Can be measured by spirometry
Physiology.exp:
Spirometry measures only the lung volumes and capacities that do not include residual volume (RV).

Vital capacity (VC) is:

VC = IRV + TV + ERV

Since it does not include RV, it can be measured directly by spirometry.

High-Yield Spirometry

Lung Volume/Capacity Measured by Spirometry?
Tidal volume (TV) ✔️ Yes
Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) ✔️ Yes
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) ✔️ Yes
Vital capacity (VC) ✔️ Yes
Residual volume (RV) ❌ No
Functional residual capacity (FRC) ❌ No
Total lung capacity (TLC) ❌ No

Rapid Recall

Spirometry measures: TV, IRV, ERV, IC, VC

Cannot measure: RV, FRC, TLC (because all include RV).

Physiology.question: ৫৩) Which are the major sites of resistance of circulation?
Physiology.exp:
Arterioles are the major resistance vessels of the circulation. They have a small radius and a thick layer of smooth muscle, allowing them to markedly alter vascular resistance through vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

According to Poiseuille's law, resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the vessel radius (R ∝ 1/r⁴). Thus, small changes in arteriolar diameter produce large changes in total peripheral resistance (TPR) and blood pressure.

High-Yield Vessel Functions

Vessel Main Function
Arteries Conduct blood under high pressure
Arterioles Major resistance vessels
Capillaries Exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste
Veins Capacitance (blood reservoir) vessels

Rapid Recall

  • Arterioles = Resistance vessels

  • Veins = Capacitance vessels

  • Capillaries = Exchange vessels

  • Aorta & large arteries = Conducting vessels

Physiology.question: ৫৪) Maximum % of total blood that can be removed with almost no effect on cardiac output?
Physiology.exp:
In a healthy person, up to about 10% of the total blood volume can be removed with little or no effect on cardiac output because compensatory mechanisms (especially sympathetic activation and venoconstriction) maintain venous return and stroke volume.

When blood loss exceeds 10–15%, cardiac output begins to decline, and signs of compensated hemorrhagic shock may appear.

High-Yield Points

Blood loss (% of blood volume) Physiological effect
≤10% Minimal or no change in cardiac output
10–15% Compensatory sympathetic responses begin
15–30% Decreased cardiac output, tachycardia, vasoconstriction
>30–40% Severe hemorrhagic shock

Rapid Recall

  • Up to 10% blood loss → Cardiac output nearly unchanged.

  • Arterial blood donation (~450–500 mL ≈ 10% of blood volume) is generally well tolerated in healthy adults.

Physiology.question: ৫৫) The average blood volume of adults is about ... of body weight?
Physiology.exp:
The average blood volume in adults is approximately 7% of body weight, which corresponds to about 70 mL/kg.

Examples:

  • 70 kg adult: ≈ 5 L of blood (70 × 70 = 4900 mL)

  • 60 kg adult: ≈ 4.2 L of blood

High-Yield Points

Parameter Normal Value
Blood volume (adult) ≈7% of body weight
Blood volume per kg ≈70 mL/kg
Average adult male ≈5–5.5 L
Average adult female ≈4–4.5 L

Rapid Recall

  • Blood volume = 7% of body weight = 70 mL/kg

  • 70 kg adult ≈ 5 L of blood

Physiology.question: ৫৬) Highest capacity of reabsorption
Physiology.exp:
The Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) has the highest reabsorptive capacity in the nephron. It reabsorbs approximately:

  • 65–70% of filtered Na⁺ and water

  • ~100% of glucose (under normal conditions)

  • ~100% of amino acids

  • 80–90% of HCO₃⁻

  • Significant amounts of phosphate, potassium, and other solutes.

This high capacity is due to its brush border (microvilli), abundant mitochondria, and extensive transport mechanisms.

High-Yield Reabsorption

Nephron Segment Major Function
PCT Maximum bulk reabsorption (≈65–70%)
Loop of Henle Countercurrent multiplier; NaCl and water handling
DCT Fine regulation of Na⁺, Ca²⁺
Collecting duct ADH- and aldosterone-dependent water and Na⁺ reabsorption

Rapid Recall

  • PCT = Maximum reabsorption

  • Ascending LOH = Diluting segment (water-impermeable)

  • DCT = Ca²⁺ reabsorption (PTH)

  • Collecting duct = ADH acts here

Physiology.question: ৫৭) Dehydration increases the plasma concentration of all the following hormones except -?
Physiology.exp:
During dehydration, there is decreased plasma volume and increased plasma osmolality. This activates mechanisms to conserve water and sodium:

  • Vasopressin (ADH) ↑ → increases water reabsorption.

  • Aldosterone ↑ → increases sodium (and water) reabsorption.

  • Norepinephrine ↑ → sympathetic activation causes vasoconstriction and helps maintain blood pressure.

  • Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) decreases, because reduced atrial stretch leads to reduced ANP secretion.

Thus, ANP is the exception—its plasma concentration does not increase during dehydration.

High-Yield Hormonal Changes in Dehydration

Hormone Change
ADH (Vasopressin) ↑
Aldosterone ↑
Norepinephrine ↑
Renin ↑
Angiotensin II ↑
ANP ↓

Rapid Recall

  • Dehydration → ↑ ADH, ↑ Renin, ↑ Angiotensin II, ↑ Aldosterone, ↑ Sympathetic activity

  • Dehydration → ↓ ANP (due to decreased atrial stretch)

Physiology.question: ৫৮) Which one of following is not a lysosomal enzyme-?
Physiology.exp:
Lysosomes contain numerous acid hydrolases that digest proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates. Examples include:

  • Cathepsins → Proteases

  • Phospholipases → Digest phospholipids

  • Arylsulfatases → Remove sulfate groups from complex molecules

Coagulase is not a lysosomal enzyme. It is an enzyme produced by Staphylococcus aureus that converts fibrinogen to fibrin and is used as a virulence factor.

High-Yield Lysosomal Enzymes

Enzyme Function
Cathepsins Protein degradation
Phospholipases Lipid degradation
Arylsulfatases Sulfate ester degradation
Acid phosphatase Phosphate ester hydrolysis
β-Glucuronidase Carbohydrate degradation

Rapid Recall

  • Lysosome = Acid hydrolases

  • Cathepsins = Proteases

  • Coagulase = Staphylococcus aureus enzyme, not lysosomal

Physiology.question: ৫৯) Which one of following is an example of secondary active counter transport-?
Physiology.exp:
Secondary active countertransport (antiport) uses the energy stored in the Na⁺ gradient (created by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) to move another substance in the opposite direction.

  • Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX) is a classic example:

    • Na⁺ enters the cell.

    • Ca²⁺ leaves the cell.

    • This is secondary active antiport (countertransport).

High-Yield Transport Mechanisms

Transporter Type
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase Primary active transport
Na⁺–Glucose (SGLT) Secondary active cotransport (symport)
Na⁺–Amino acid Secondary active cotransport (symport)
Na⁺–Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCX) Secondary active countertransport (antiport)

Rapid Recall

  • Symport = Same direction: Na⁺–glucose, Na⁺–amino acid.

  • Antiport = Opposite direction: Na⁺–Ca²⁺, Na⁺–H⁺.

  • Na⁺/K⁺ pump = Primary active (ATP-dependent).

Physiology.question: ৬০) Normal quiet breathing is accomplished almost entirely by movement of the
Physiology.exp:
During normal quiet breathing (eupnea), inspiration is accomplished almost entirely by contraction of the diaphragm.

  • Diaphragm contracts and descends → increases the vertical diameter of the thoracic cavity → intrathoracic pressure falls → air enters the lungs.

  • Quiet expiration is passive, resulting from elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall.

High-Yield Respiratory Muscles

Muscle Function
Diaphragm Main muscle of quiet inspiration
External intercostals Assist inspiration
Internal intercostals Forced expiration (interosseous part)
Abdominal muscles (e.g., rectus abdominis) Forced expiration

Rapid Recall

  • Quiet inspiration → Diaphragm

  • Quiet expiration → Passive (elastic recoil)

  • Forced inspiration → SCM, scalenes, external intercostals

  • Forced expiration → Internal intercostals + abdominal muscles

Physiology.question: ৬১) Which initiates cardiac cycle
Physiology.exp:
The cardiac cycle begins with atrial systole, which is initiated by the SA node. Atrial contraction completes ventricular filling by delivering the final 20–30% ("atrial kick") of blood into the ventricles before ventricular systole begins.

Sequence of the cardiac cycle:

  1. Atrial systole ✔️ (starts the cycle)

  2. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction

  3. Ventricular ejection

  4. Isovolumetric relaxation

  5. Ventricular filling (rapid filling → diastasis)

High-Yield Points

  • Pacemaker: SA node

  • Cardiac cycle starts with: Atrial systole

  • "Atrial kick" contributes: ~20–30% of ventricular filling.

Physiology.question: ৬২) Utilization of O2 by tissues is reduced in which form of hypoxia?
Physiology.exp:
In histotoxic hypoxia, the tissues are unable to utilize oxygen despite adequate oxygen delivery. This occurs because cellular oxidative enzymes (especially cytochrome oxidase) are inhibited.

Example: Cyanide poisoning.

High-Yield Types of Hypoxia

Type Primary Defect Example
Hypoxic ↓ Arterial PO₂ High altitude, COPD
Anaemic ↓ O₂-carrying capacity Anemia, CO poisoning
Stagnant (Circulatory) ↓ Tissue perfusion Shock, heart failure
Histotoxic ↓ Tissue utilization of O₂ Cyanide poisoning

Rapid Recall

  • Hypoxic = Low PO₂

  • Anaemic = Low Hb

  • Stagnant = Low blood flow

  • Histotoxic = Cells cannot use O₂ (cyanide)

Physiology.question: ৬৩) A person with … frequently has cyanosis?
Physiology.exp:
Cyanosis becomes clinically apparent when deoxygenated hemoglobin exceeds ~5 g/dL in capillary blood.

  • Polycythaemia increases the total hemoglobin concentration, so even with a normal percentage of oxygen saturation, the absolute amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin can easily exceed 5 g/dL, making cyanosis more frequent.

High-Yield Points

  • Cyanosis appears when reduced Hb > 5 g/dL.

  • Polycythaemia → Cyanosis more likely.

  • Anaemia → Cyanosis less likely despite severe hypoxemia.

Rapid Recall

  • Polycythaemia = More cyanosis

  • Anaemia = Less cyanosis

  • Cyanosis depends on absolute deoxygenated Hb, not just oxygen saturation.

Physiology.exp: Reference: Guyton 14th; P- 526

Physiology.question: ৬৫) BP on arm is measured over
Physiology.exp:
Blood pressure in the arm is routinely measured over the brachial artery using a sphygmomanometer.

  • The cuff is placed around the upper arm.

  • The stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the antecubital fossa to hear the Korotkoff sounds.

High-Yield Points

  • Routine arm BP measurement → Brachial artery

  • Pulse commonly palpated → Radial artery

  • Popliteal artery → BP measurement in the leg

Rapid Recall

  • Arm BP = Brachial artery

  • Wrist pulse = Radial artery

  • Leg BP = Popliteal artery

Physiology.question: ৬৬) Im absence of vasopressin, the greatest fraction of filtered water is reabsorbed in the-?
Physiology.exp:
Even in the absence of vasopressin (ADH), the Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) continues to reabsorb the greatest fraction of filtered water.

  • PCT reabsorbs ~65–70% of filtered water obligatorily (independent of ADH).

  • Descending limb of Loop of Henle (DLLH) also reabsorbs water but much less (~10–15%).

  • Ascending limb of Loop of Henle (ALLH) is impermeable to water.

  • Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT) reabsorbs little water without ADH.

High-Yield Water Reabsorption

Nephron Segment Water Reabsorbed ADH Dependence
PCT 65–70% No (obligatory)
Descending limb 10–15% No
Ascending limb 0% Water impermeable
DCT & Collecting duct Variable Yes (ADH-dependent)

Rapid Recall

  • PCT = Maximum obligatory water reabsorption (~65–70%)

  • Descending limb = Water permeable

  • Ascending limb = Water impermeable

  • ADH acts mainly on late DCT and collecting duct

Physiology.question: ৬৭) Net filtration pressure in glomerulus (mmHg)
Physiology.exp:
The net filtration pressure (NFP) in the glomerulus is the pressure that drives filtration from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule.

Calculation:

  • Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PGC) = 60 mmHg

  • Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure (PBS) = 18 mmHg

  • Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (πGC) = 32 mmHg

NFP = PGC − (PBS + πGC)

= 60 − (18 + 32)

= 10 mmHg

High-Yield Pressures

Pressure Value (mmHg)
Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure 60
Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure 18
Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure 32
Net filtration pressure 10

Rapid Recall

  • 60 − 18 − 32 = 10 mmHg

  • Hydrostatic pressure favors filtration

  • Bowman's pressure and plasma oncotic pressure oppose filtration

Physiology.question: ৬৮) Clearance rate is maximum for
৬৯) Which decreases NaCl reabsorption?
৭০) Erythropoietin is secreted from
Physiology.exp:
Erythropoietin (EPO) is produced predominantly by the kidneys (about 90%) from peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the renal cortex and outer medulla in response to hypoxia. It stimulates erythropoiesis in the bone marrow.

High-Yield Points

  • Adult: Kidney → ~90% of EPO

  • Fetus: Liver is the major source.

  • Stimulus: Hypoxia → ↑ EPO → ↑ RBC production

Rapid Recall

  • EPO = Kidney

  • Fetal EPO = Liver

  • Target = Bone marrow

Physiology.question: ৭১) The extrinsic pathway is assessed by...
Physiology.exp:
The extrinsic coagulation pathway is assessed by Prothrombin Time (PT).

  • PT evaluates the extrinsic (Factor VII) and common pathway (Factors X, V, II, I).

  • It is used to monitor warfarin therapy (reported as INR).

High-Yield Coagulation Tests

Test Pathway Assessed
PT (INR) Extrinsic + Common
APTT Intrinsic + Common
BT Platelet function
CT Whole coagulation (obsolete, nonspecific)

Rapid Recall

  • PT → Extrinsic → Factor VII → Warfarin

  • APTT → Intrinsic → Heparin

  • BT → Platelets

Physiology.question: ৭২) Key reaction of coagulation in each pathway is
Physiology.exp:
The intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge at the activation of Factor X (Xa). This is the key reaction in the coagulation cascade, leading to the common pathway:

  • Factor X → Xa

  • Xa converts Prothrombin (Factor II) → Thrombin (IIa)

  • Thrombin converts Fibrinogen (Factor I) → Fibrin

High-Yield Coagulation Cascade

  • Intrinsic: XII → XI → IX + VIII → X

  • Extrinsic: VII + Tissue Factor → X

  • Common: X → II → I (Fibrin)

Rapid Recall

  • Convergence point = Factor X

  • PT → Extrinsic (VII)

  • APTT → Intrinsic (XII, XI, IX, VIII)

  • Factor Xa → Prothrombin → Thrombin → Fibrin

Physiology.question: ৭৩) INR in a healthy person -
Physiology.exp:
The International Normalized Ratio (INR) standardizes the Prothrombin Time (PT) across laboratories.

  • In a healthy individual, the normal INR is approximately 0.9–1.2, and many exam texts accept 0.9–1.3.

High-Yield INR Values

INR Interpretation
0.9–1.3 Normal
2.0–3.0 Therapeutic for most warfarin indications
2.5–3.5 Mechanical mitral valve (many guidelines)
>4.5 Increased bleeding risk

Rapid Recall

  • Normal INR = 0.9–1.3

  • Warfarin monitoring = PT/INR

  • Target INR (most indications) = 2.0–3.0

Physiology.question: ৭৪) Which blood group has no antigen
Physiology.exp:
In the ABO blood group system:

  • Group A → A antigen on RBCs

  • Group B → B antigen on RBCs

  • Group AB → Both A and B antigens

  • Group O → Neither A nor B antigens

Thus, blood group O has no A or B antigen on the red blood cell surface.

The corresponding antibodies in plasma are:

  • A → Anti-B

  • B → Anti-A

  • AB → No anti-A or anti-B

  • O → Both anti-A and anti-B

High-Yield ABO Table

Blood Group RBC Antigen Plasma Antibody
A A Anti-B
B B Anti-A
AB A + B None
O None Anti-A + Anti-B

Rapid Recall

  • O = No A/B antigen

  • AB = No antibody (universal recipient)

  • O negative = Universal RBC donor

Physiology.question: ৭৫) Which play an important role in the defence mechanism of the body against the parasites?
Physiology.exp:
Eosinophils are the principal leukocytes involved in defense against parasitic (especially helminthic) infections. They kill parasites by releasing cytotoxic granule proteins, including:

  • Major Basic Protein (MBP)

  • Eosinophil Cationic Protein (ECP)

  • Eosinophil Peroxidase (EPO)

They are also involved in allergic diseases such as asthma and allergic rhinitis.

High-Yield Functions of WBCs

Cell Main Function
Neutrophils Bacterial infections
Eosinophils Parasites, allergy
Basophils Histamine release, allergy
Monocytes Macrophages, phagocytosis
Lymphocytes Adaptive immunity

Rapid Recall

  • Parasites → Eosinophils

  • Bacteria → Neutrophils

  • Allergy (histamine) → Basophils

  • Chronic inflammation → Monocytes/Macrophages

Physiology.question: ৭৬) Factor decreasing ESR
Physiology.exp:
Increased blood viscosity slows the settling of red blood cells, thereby decreasing the ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate).

High-Yield Factors

Increase ESR

  • Rouleaux formation

  • Increased fibrinogen/immunoglobulins

  • Pregnancy

  • Anemia

  • Macrocytosis

Decrease ESR

  • Increased blood viscosity

  • Polycythemia

  • Sickle cells, spherocytes (abnormal RBC shape)

  • Microcytosis

Rapid Recall

  • Rouleaux → ESR ↑

  • Blood viscosity ↑ → ESR ↓

  • Polycythemia → ESR ↓

Physiology.question: ৭৭) Renin also known as angiotensinogenase is circulating enzyme released mainly by JG cells in the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidneys plasma renin levels are decreased in patients with-?
Physiology.exp:
Renin is secreted by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the kidney in response to:

  • ↓ Renal perfusion pressure

  • ↓ NaCl delivery to the macula densa

  • β₁-adrenergic stimulation

In primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), autonomous aldosterone secretion causes:

  • Na⁺ and water retention

  • Expansion of extracellular fluid volume

  • Suppression of renin release via negative feedback

Therefore, plasma renin is low.

High-Yield Table

Condition Plasma Renin
Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) ↓
Secondary hyperaldosteronism ↑
Renal artery stenosis ↑
Heart failure ↑
Salt restriction ↑

Rapid Recall

  • Primary hyperaldosteronism → ↓ Renin, ↑ Aldosterone

  • Secondary hyperaldosteronism → ↑ Renin, ↑ Aldosterone

  • Renal artery stenosis → High renin

  • Heart failure → High renin

Physiology.question: ৭৮) Secretion of K+ by the distal tubule will be decreased by -
Physiology.exp:
Potassium (K⁺) secretion occurs mainly in the late distal tubule and cortical collecting duct by principal cells. It is increased by:

  • Aldosterone

  • High K⁺ intake

  • Increased distal Na⁺ delivery

  • Metabolic alkalosis

Spironolactone is an aldosterone receptor antagonist. By blocking aldosterone, it:

  • ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption

  • ↓ K⁺ secretion

  • Causes potassium retention (hyperkalemia)

Therefore, it decreases K⁺ secretion.

High-Yield

Increases K⁺ secretion

  • Aldosterone

  • High K⁺ diet

  • Metabolic alkalosis

  • Increased distal tubular flow/Na⁺ delivery

Decreases K⁺ secretion

  • Spironolactone

  • Hypoaldosteronism

  • Metabolic acidosis

Rapid Recall

  • Aldosterone → Na⁺ retained, K⁺ excreted

  • Spironolactone → K⁺-sparing diuretic

  • Hyperaldosteronism → Hypokalemia

  • Spironolactone → Risk of hyperkalemia

Physiology.question: ৭৯) Which of the following causes a decrease in renal Ca2+ clearance?
Physiology.exp:
Thiazide diuretics (e.g., chlorothiazide) decrease renal Ca²⁺ clearance by increasing Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). This results in reduced urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria).

High-Yield

Condition/Drug Renal Ca²⁺ Clearance
Thiazides (chlorothiazide) ↓
Loop diuretics (furosemide) ↑
Hypoparathyroidism ↑
ECF volume expansion ↑
PTH ↓ (↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption)

Rapid Recall

  • Thiazides → "Save Ca²⁺" (↓ urinary calcium)

  • Loop diuretics → "Lose Ca²⁺" (↑ urinary calcium)

  • PTH → ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption → ↓ Ca²⁺ clearance

Physiology.question: ৮০) Amino acid required for thyroid hormone synthesis
৮১) Tetany occurs when plasma calcium level falls below …mg/dl
Physiology.exp:
Tetany occurs when the plasma ionized calcium concentration decreases, increasing the excitability of nerves and muscles. Clinically, tetany usually develops when the total plasma calcium falls below approximately 6 mg/dL (1.5 mmol/L).

High-Yield

  • Normal total serum calcium: 8.5–10.5 mg/dL

  • Tetany: Usually when total serum calcium <6 mg/dL

  • Normal ionized calcium: 4.5–5.6 mg/dL (1.1–1.3 mmol/L)

Rapid Recall

  • Tetany → Hypocalcemia

  • Threshold for tetany ≈ Total Ca²⁺ <6 mg/dL

  • Clinical signs: Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, carpopedal spasm.

Physiology.question: ৮২) The most active adrenal androgen is
Physiology.exp:
The adrenal cortex (mainly the zona reticularis) secretes several androgens:

  • Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) – weak androgen

  • Androstenedione – weak androgen

  • Small amounts of Testosterone – the most biologically active androgen

Although DHEA is the major adrenal androgen secreted quantitatively, testosterone is the most potent (most active) adrenal androgen.

High-Yield

Hormone Androgenic Activity
Testosterone Most active (most potent)
Androstenedione Weak
DHEA Weak
DHEA-S Very weak

Rapid Recall

  • Zona reticularis → Androgens

  • Most abundant adrenal androgen → DHEA

  • Most active androgen → Testosterone

Physiology.question: ৮৩) B cell of islets of Langerhans secrete
Physiology.exp:
The β (beta) cells of the islets of Langerhans synthesize and secrete insulin, the hormone responsible for lowering blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake and storage.

High-Yield Islet Cells

Cell Hormone
α (Alpha) Glucagon
β (Beta) Insulin
δ (Delta) Somatostatin
PP (F) cells Pancreatic polypeptide (PP)

Rapid Recall

  • β = Insulin

  • α = Glucagon

  • δ = Somatostatin

  • PP (F) = Pancreatic polypeptide

Physiology.question: ৮৪) Which of the following substances has the highest renal clearance?
Physiology.exp:
Renal clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance by the kidneys per unit time.

PAH has the highest renal clearance because it is:

  • Freely filtered at the glomerulus.

  • Actively secreted by the proximal tubule.

  • Almost completely removed from the plasma in a single pass through the kidneys (at low plasma concentrations).

High-Yield Clearance Values

Substance Renal Clearance
PAH Highest (~Renal Plasma Flow ≈ 600 mL/min)
Inulin GFR (~125 mL/min)
Creatinine Slightly > GFR
Na⁺ Very low
Glucose ~0

Rapid Recall

  • PAH → Renal Plasma Flow (highest clearance)

  • Inulin → GFR

  • Creatinine → Estimates GFR

  • Glucose → Clearance = 0 (normally)

Physiology.question: ৮৫) Which of the following is a cause of metabolic alkalosis?
Physiology.exp:
Hyperaldosteronism causes metabolic alkalosis because aldosterone increases:

  • H⁺ secretion by α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct.

  • K⁺ secretion, leading to hypokalemia, which further promotes alkalosis.

The result is metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia.

High-Yield

Causes of Metabolic Alkalosis

  • Hyperaldosteronism

  • Vomiting / nasogastric suction

  • Loop and thiazide diuretics

  • Excess alkali intake (milk-alkali syndrome)

Causes of Metabolic Acidosis

  • Chronic renal failure

  • Ethylene glycol, methanol

  • Diarrhea

  • Acetazolamide

  • Diabetic ketoacidosis

Rapid Recall

  • Aldosterone → H⁺ secretion ↑ → Metabolic alkalosis

  • Acetazolamide → HCO₃⁻ loss → Metabolic acidosis

  • Ethylene glycol → High anion gap metabolic acidosis

  • CKD → Metabolic acidosis

Physiology.question: ৮৬) A raised blood pH & Bicarbonate level is consistent with-?
Physiology.option2: Chronic renal failure with raised PC02
Physiology.exp:
A raised blood pH together with a raised plasma bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) indicates primary metabolic alkalosis.

Persistent vomiting causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), resulting in:

  • ↑ Blood pH

  • ↑ Plasma HCO₃⁻

  • Compensatory ↑ PCO₂ due to hypoventilation

High-Yield Acid–Base Patterns

Disorder pH HCO₃⁻ PCO₂
Metabolic alkalosis ↑ ↑ ↑ (compensation)
Respiratory alkalosis ↑ ↓ (compensation) ↓
Metabolic acidosis ↓ ↓ ↓ (compensation)
Respiratory acidosis ↓ ↑ (compensation) ↑

Rapid Recall

  • Vomiting → Loss of HCl → Metabolic alkalosis

  • Metabolic alkalosis = ↑ pH + ↑ HCO₃⁻

  • Respiratory alkalosis = ↑ pH + ↓ PCO₂ + ↓ HCO₃⁻ (compensated)

Physiology.question: ৮৭) Excess Catecholamine causes-
Physiology.exp:
Phaeochromocytoma is a tumor of the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla that secretes excessive catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine).

Clinical features:

  • Hypertension (often paroxysmal)

  • Headache

  • Palpitations

  • Profuse sweating

  • Tremor and anxiety

High-Yield

  • Catecholamine excess → Phaeochromocytoma

  • Diagnosis: ↑ Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines/catecholamines

  • Treatment: α-blockade first (e.g., phenoxybenzamine), then β-blocker if needed.

Rapid Recall

  • 5 Ps of Phaeochromocytoma: Pressure (HTN), Pain (headache), Perspiration, Palpitations, Pallor

  • Never start a β-blocker before adequate α-blockade.

Physiology.question: ৮৮) Hyposecretion of cortisol produce-
Physiology.exp:
Hyposecretion of cortisol results in Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency).

Features of Addison's disease:

  • ↓ Cortisol

  • Fatigue, weakness

  • Weight loss

  • Hypotension

  • Hyperpigmentation (due to ↑ ACTH in primary adrenal insufficiency)

  • Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia (because of associated aldosterone deficiency)

High-Yield

Disorder Hormone Excess/Deficiency
Addison's disease ↓ Cortisol (± ↓ Aldosterone)
Cushing's syndrome ↑ Cortisol
Conn's syndrome ↑ Aldosterone
Phaeochromocytoma ↑ Catecholamines

Rapid Recall

  • ↓ Cortisol → Addison's disease

  • ↑ Cortisol → Cushing's syndrome

  • ↑ Aldosterone → Conn's syndrome

  • ↑ Catecholamines → Phaeochromocytoma

Physiology.question: ৮৯) The percentage of TBW is highest in...
Physiology.exp:
Total Body Water (TBW) as a percentage of body weight is highest in newborns because they have:

  • Higher extracellular fluid (ECF) volume.

  • Lower body fat content than adults.

High-Yield TBW Values

Group TBW (% of Body Weight)
Newborn 75–80%
Infant 65–70%
Adult male ~60%
Adult female ~50–55%
Elderly ~45–50%

Rapid Recall

  • Highest TBW → Newborn (75–80%)

  • Adult male → 60%

  • Adult female → 50–55%

  • Lowest TBW → Elderly

Physiology.question: ৯০) Normal GFR is ....L/day?
Physiology.exp:
The normal Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult is approximately:

  • 125 mL/min

Converting to liters per day:

  • 125 mL/min × 60 min/hour × 24 hours/day

  • = 180,000 mL/day

  • = 180 L/day

Parameter Normal Value
GFR 125 mL/min
GFR/day 180 L/day
Renal plasma flow (RPF) ~600 mL/min
Renal blood flow (RBF) ~1200 mL/min
Urine output 1–2 L/day

  • GFR = 125 mL/min = 180 L/day

  • Inulin clearance = GFR

  • Creatinine clearance ≈ GFR

  • PAH clearance ≈ Renal Plasma Flow (RPF)

Physiology.question: ৯১) Micelle formation is necessary for the intestinal absorption of
Physiology.exp:
Micelles, formed by bile salts, are essential for the intestinal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and lipid digestion products (fatty acids, monoglycerides, cholesterol).

Therefore, Vitamin D requires micelle formation for efficient absorption.

High-Yield

  • Micelles are required for absorption of:

    • Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K

    • Long-chain fatty acids

    • Monoglycerides

    • Cholesterol

  • Do NOT require micelles:

    • Glucose

    • Galactose

    • Amino acids

    • Short- and medium-chain fatty acids

Rapid Recall

  • Micelles = Bile salts + Lipids

  • Micelles → Absorption of ADEK

  • Terminal ileum → Bile acid reabsorption (enterohepatic circulation)

Physiology.question: ৯২) Which hormone has receptor on cytoplasm?
৯৩) Which stimulates secretion of uterine milk?
৯৪) Excess GH secretion during adulthood may result in
৯৫) A fall in plasma Na+ concentration -?
Physiology.option1: results from excessive production of ADH
Physiology.exp:
Reference- Rodde physiology/6th/Q-48

A fall in plasma Na⁺ concentration (hyponatremia) commonly results from excessive secretion of ADH (SIADH). ADH causes increased water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, leading to dilution of plasma sodium.

The other options:

  • খ) Decreases intracellular fluid volume ❌ False. Hyponatremia decreases plasma osmolality, causing water to move into cells, thereby increasing intracellular fluid volume.

  • গ) Increases plasma osmolarity ❌ False. Hyponatremia decreases plasma osmolarity.

  • ঘ) Is likely to cause thirst ❌ False. Thirst is primarily stimulated by increased plasma osmolality (hypernatremia), not hyponatremia.

High-Yield

Hyponatremia Effect
Plasma Na⁺ ↓ Plasma osmolality ↓
Water movement ECF → ICF
Intracellular volume ↑
Common cause SIADH (↑ ADH)

Rapid Recall

  • ↑ ADH → Water retention → Dilutional hyponatremia

  • Hyponatremia → ↓ Plasma osmolality → Cellular swelling (especially brain)

  • Hypernatremia, not hyponatremia, is the major stimulus for thirst.

Physiology.question: ৯৬) What is not the endogenous causes of Normochloremic metabolic acidosis-?
Physiology.exp:
Normochloremic metabolic acidosis is another term for high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA). It is caused by the accumulation of endogenous acids.

Endogenous causes of normochloremic (high anion gap) metabolic acidosis:

  • Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) ✔

  • Lactic acidosis ✔

  • Renal failure (uremia) ✔

Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) ❌ causes hyperchloremic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis, due to impaired renal acid secretion or bicarbonate reabsorption, without accumulation of unmeasured acids.

High-Yield

Disorder Type of Metabolic Acidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis High anion gap (Normochloremic)
Lactic acidosis High anion gap (Normochloremic)
Renal failure High anion gap (Normochloremic)

Rapid Recall

Physiology.question: ৯৭) Biochemical changes occur following prolonged vomiting are-?
Physiology.exp:
Prolonged vomiting causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), leading to:

  • Metabolic alkalosis

  • Hypochloremia

  • Hypokalemia (due to renal potassium loss secondary to volume depletion and increased aldosterone)

Therefore, hypokalemia is the characteristic biochemical change.

High-Yield

Prolonged Vomiting →

  • Metabolic alkalosis

  • Hypochloremia

  • Hypokalemia

  • Volume depletion

  • Secondary hyperaldosteronism

Rapid Recall

  • Vomiting = Lose HCl → Metabolic alkalosis

  • Vomiting = ↓ Cl⁻ + ↓ K⁺

  • Diarrhea = Metabolic acidosis

Physiology.question: ৯৮) Hormones responsible for K+ driven into cell excludes-?
Physiology.exp:
The hormones that promote the movement of K⁺ from the extracellular fluid into cells are:

  • Insulin ✔ – Stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, rapidly shifting K⁺ into cells.

  • Epinephrine (β₂-adrenergic effect) ✔ – Activates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, driving K⁺ intracellularly.

  • Aldosterone ✔ – Increases intracellular K⁺ uptake and enhances renal K⁺ excretion.

Glucagon does not promote intracellular K⁺ uptake and is not used in the physiological regulation of potassium distribution.

High-Yield

Hormones that shift K⁺ into cells:

  • Insulin

  • β₂-adrenergic agonists (Epinephrine)

  • Aldosterone

Hormones that do not:

  • Glucagon

Rapid Recall

  • Insulin → K⁺ into cells

  • β₂ stimulation (Epinephrine) → K⁺ into cells

  • Aldosterone → K⁺ into cells + ↑ renal K⁺ excretion

  • Glucagon → No significant effect on K⁺ shift

Physiology.question: ৯৯) Plateau phase in action potential of cardiac muscle due to-
Physiology.option1: Is due to efflux of K+
Physiology.option2: Is due to fast sodium channel
Physiology.option3: Is due to slow Ca+ Na channel
Physiology.exp:
The plateau phase (Phase 2) of the ventricular cardiac action potential is produced mainly by:

  • Opening of slow L-type Ca²⁺ channels (historically called slow Ca²⁺–Na⁺ channels in Guyton), allowing prolonged Ca²⁺ influx.

  • Simultaneously, there is reduced K⁺ efflux, which helps maintain the plateau.

Phase Main Ion Movement
0 Fast Na⁺ influx (depolarization)
1 Transient K⁺ efflux
2 (Plateau) Slow Ca²⁺ influx (L-type channels) with ↓ K⁺ efflux
3 K⁺ efflux (repolarization)
4 Resting membrane potential

Rapid Recall

  • Phase 0 → Fast Na⁺

  • Phase 2 (Plateau) → Slow Ca²⁺ (L-type) channels

  • Phase 3 → K⁺ efflux

  • Plateau = Ventricular systole

Physiology.question: ১০০) Upper motor neuron inhibits Lower motor neuron by releasing-?
Physiology.exp:
Reference-Ganong physiology/26th/P-143

Upper motor neurons (UMNs) do not directly inhibit lower motor neurons (LMNs). Instead, they activate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, which release glycine (and in some pathways GABA). Glycine is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and suppresses LMN activity.

High-Yield

Neurotransmitter Main Action
Glycine Inhibitory (spinal cord, interneurons)
GABA Inhibitory (brain)
Glutamate Excitatory (CNS)
Acetylcholine Excitatory at neuromuscular junction

Rapid Recall

  • Spinal cord inhibition → Glycine

  • Brain inhibition → GABA

  • UMN lesions → Loss of inhibitory influence → Hyperreflexia, spasticity

  • LMN → Acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
